subtitle: Decide which surface is in front, then decide how bright it looks.

hsr.body:
Stand in front of a wall with a vase on a table. Do you see the back of the vase? No, because something nearer is in the way. A renderer must make the same decision: when objects overlap, only the nearest surface along each line of sight may be drawn.

There are two schools. Object-space methods compare polygons geometrically (the painter’s algorithm); image-space methods decide per pixel. And a cheap first filter is back-face detection: a face is hidden if its normal N and the view vector V satisfy N·V > 0, which removes roughly half the faces of a closed solid.

Try one. A face has normal N = (0, 0, −1); the viewer looks along V = (0, 0, −1) (into the screen). N·V = (0)(0) + (0)(0) + (−1)(−1) = 1 > 0, so the face points away from the viewer: back-facing, cull it.
keynotes: Only the nearest surface along each line of sight may be drawn.
Object-space methods compare polygons geometrically (painter’s algorithm); image-space methods decide per pixel.
Back-face detection hides a face if N·V > 0, roughly half the faces of a closed solid.
N = (0,0,−1) and V = (0,0,−1) give N·V = 1 > 0, so the face is culled.

z.body:
Here is one of the most elegant ideas in graphics, and it fits in one sentence: remember, for every pixel, how close the nearest thing you have drawn there is. That memory is the Z-buffer.

Start with depth = ∞. For each polygon and each pixel it covers, compute the depth z; if z is smaller (nearer) than the stored value, write the colour and the new depth. Otherwise skip it. Polygons can arrive in any order, so there is no sorting, and it is simple in hardware. The cost is O(pixels × overlapping surfaces), plus one depth value per pixel. The A-buffer adds transparency; scan-line methods handle one row at a time. Follow the test-and-write loop in the figure. And what does a Z-buffer store, per pixel? The depth of the nearest surface so far.
keynotes: The Z-buffer keeps, for every pixel, the depth of the nearest surface drawn so far, starting at ∞.
A fragment is written only if its z is nearer than the stored value, so polygons can arrive in any order.
The cost is O(pixels × overlapping surfaces) and one depth value per pixel; the A-buffer adds transparency.

light.body:
Now that we know what is visible, how bright should it be? Think of a ball in a sunlit room: it has a general glow from the room, a matte brightness that fades as the surface turns away from the lamp, and a shiny spot where the lamp is reflected. That is the Phong model, adding three terms.

Ambient I = kₐ is light from everywhere. Diffuse kd·cos θ (Lambert) is proportional to the angle between the normal and the light, which is what makes matte surfaces. Specular ks·cosⁿ α is the highlight where the reflection points at the eye, and a larger n means a tighter, shinier spot. With ka = 0.1, kd = 0.5, ks = 0.4, n = 10, a surface lit head-on has I = 0.1 + 0.5·1 + 0.4·1 = 1; at 60° it drops to 0.35. Increasing the exponent n makes the highlight smaller. The three frames add the terms one at a time.
keynotes: The Phong model sums ambient (kₐ), diffuse (kd·cos θ) and specular (ks·cosⁿ α) terms.
A larger exponent n gives a tighter, shinier highlight.
With ka = 0.1, kd = 0.5, ks = 0.4, n = 10, head-on I = 1 and at 60° it drops to 0.35.

shade.body:
Running the full lighting formula at every pixel would be slow, so cheaper ways were invented, each trading speed for quality. Constant (flat) shading gives one intensity per polygon, so the surface looks faceted like a cut gem. Gouraud computes intensity at the vertices and interpolates across the polygon, which looks smooth but can miss highlights that fall inside a polygon. Phong shading interpolates the normals and applies the illumination model per pixel, which gives accurate highlights at a higher cost.

As the figure says, cost and quality both rise left to right. So Gouraud shading interpolates intensities (colours); Phong interpolates normals. Keep that difference straight and you will not mix the two up in an exam.
keynotes: Constant (flat) shading gives one intensity per polygon and a faceted look.
Gouraud computes intensity at the vertices and interpolates, which is smooth but can miss highlights inside a polygon.
Phong shading interpolates the normals and applies the illumination model per pixel: accurate but more expensive.

summary.body:
Here is your pocket summary.

  • Back-face: N·V > 0 → cull. Z-buffer: keep the nearest fragment per pixel.
  • Phong model = ambient + diffuse + specular; flat < Gouraud < Phong shading.

If these two lines make sense to you, so does the rest of the chapter.
keynotes: Back-face culling removes faces with N·V > 0, and the Z-buffer keeps the nearest fragment per pixel.
The Phong model is ambient + diffuse + specular, and flat < Gouraud < Phong shading.

try.body: Experiment time. Set the shininess to 80 in the figure and look at the highlight: it becomes much narrower. Now ask what happens at 60° from the normal. For a very shiny surface, the specular term has almost died away, because cosⁿ of a big angle collapses quickly when n is large. Predict first, then check it.
keynotes: Shininess 80 gives a much narrower highlight.
For very shiny surfaces the specular term at 60° from the normal is almost zero, because cosⁿ collapses quickly for large n.
